title: The boundary case
idea: MEET (thinking). The value exactly ON the cutoff is a classic edge case. 'Pass if 50 or more' must decide what 50 itself does.

exercises.prompt: A score passes if it is '50 or more.' What should a score of exactly 50 do?
exercises.explanation: '50 or more' means >= 50, so 50 passes. The value right on the boundary is the one people get wrong.

exercises.prompt: Which comparison matches 'passes if 50 or MORE'?
exercises.explanation: >= includes the boundary (50). Using > by mistake would wrongly FAIL a score of exactly 50.

exercises.prompt: The difference between > and >= only shows up at the exact boundary value.
exercises.explanation: Yes. For 49 and 51 both agree; only at 50 do > (fails) and >= (passes) differ. That's why the boundary is the edge case.

exercises.prompt: A rule says 'free shipping OVER 100.' Does an order of exactly 100 get free shipping?
exercises.explanation: 'Over 100' is > 100, so exactly 100 does NOT qualify. Words like 'over' vs 'at least' decide the boundary.

exercises.prompt: Match each English phrase to its comparison.
exercises.explanation: 'or more' and 'at least' include the boundary (>=); 'more than' and 'over' exclude it (>). Read the words carefully.

exercises.prompt: To TEST whether your cutoff is right, which input should you try first?
exercises.explanation: Test the boundary value. Values far from it rarely reveal a >/>= mix-up; the exact cutoff does.

exercises.prompt: For the rule 'child ticket if age is UNDER 12,' which ages are the tricky ones to check? (Select all.)
exercises.explanation: 11 (child) and 12 (not a child) sit right on either side of the cutoff. 3 and 50 are far away and won't catch a boundary bug.

exercises.prompt: 'At least 18' and 'over 18' mean the same thing for an 18-year-old.
exercises.explanation: No. 'At least 18' (>=) includes 18; 'over 18' (>) excludes it. For exactly 18 they disagree — a boundary difference.

exercises.prompt: REVIEW: last unit's 'is_pass' used score >= 50. Re-checking with [49, 50, 51] was testing...
options: The boundary — making sure 50 passes and 49 doesn't
exercises.explanation: Picking 49, 50, 51 targets the boundary directly. That's how you prove the cutoff behaves as the words say.

options: Decide what the value ON the cutoff does, and test the boundary itself
exercises.explanation: The boundary value is the edge case for any cutoff. Read the words ('or more' vs 'over'), pick >/>=, and test it directly.
